name: Italian Game
idea: Both sides develop naturally and fight for the center, with White's bishop eyeing f7 from c4.
plans: White prepares d4 to build a big center, supported by c3.
Black often plays d6 and O-O, then looks for ...d5 breaks later.
Piece activity and quick castling matter more than material grabs this early.

name: Ruy Lopez
idea: White pins pressure on the knight defending e5 while preparing a slow, strategic squeeze.
plans: White usually continues Re1, c3 and d4 to claim the center.
Black often replies with b5 and d6, keeping the position solid and flexible.
Games can stay tense for many moves — patience and piece placement matter more than speed.

name: Sicilian Defense
idea: Black accepts an asymmetrical pawn structure in exchange for active, unbalanced play and chances on both wings.
plans: Black's a6 prepares ...b5, gaining queenside space and hitting White's pieces.
White often attacks on the kingside with f3, Be3 and a queenside-castled setup (the 'English Attack').
Sharp, theory-heavy lines reward players comfortable with imbalanced, double-edged positions.

name: French Defense
idea: Black accepts a slightly cramped position in return for a solid pawn chain and a clear plan to strike at White's center later.
plans: Black's typical break is ...c5, challenging d4 and opening lines for the pieces.
White often gains space with e5 and attacks on the kingside.
Black's light-squared bishop is a long-term problem piece worth planning around.

name: Caro-Kann Defense
idea: Black trades in the center early and, unlike the French, gets the light-squared bishop out before closing the position.
plans: Black follows up with e6, Nf6 and a solid, easy-to-play structure.
White typically develops with Bc4 or Bd3 and aims for a small but lasting space edge.
The position is very solid for Black — great for players who like fewer weaknesses.

name: Queen's Gambit Declined
idea: Black keeps the center intact rather than grabbing the c4 pawn, aiming for a solid, well-tested structure.
plans: White pressures d5 and often expands with Rc1 and Bd3.
Black looks to free the position with ...c5 or ...dxc4 followed by ...c5 at the right moment.
A classical battleground since the 19th century — rich in strategic ideas.

name: Queen's Gambit Accepted
idea: Black grabs the c4 pawn temporarily, planning to give it back for comfortable development.
plans: White regains the pawn with Bxc4 and aims for a strong center with e4 later.
Black often plays c5 and b5 to fight for queenside space and free the position.
Development speed matters more here than holding on to the extra pawn.

name: Slav Defense
idea: Black defends d5 with the c-pawn instead of e6, keeping the light-squared bishop free to develop outside the pawn chain.
plans: Black often plays Bf5 or Bg4 early, something the QGD structure makes harder.
White tries to prove a central and development advantage before Black consolidates.
A very solid, well-respected defense at every level of chess.

name: King's Indian Defense
idea: Black allows White a big pawn center on purpose, planning to attack it later with pieces and pawn breaks.
plans: Black typically castles kingside, then plays ...e5 or ...c5 to challenge the center.
A famous plan is the kingside pawn storm with ...f5-f4 once queens castle on opposite sides.
Sharp and double-edged — both sides usually attack on opposite wings.

name: Nimzo-Indian Defense
idea: Black pins the knight on c3 immediately, fighting for the center with pieces rather than pawns.
plans: Black often follows with O-O and c5, pressuring d4 and doubling White's c-pawns if Bxc3 is played.
White chooses between Qc2, e3 or a3 setups, each leading to distinct strategic battles.
Considered one of the most reliable defenses to 1.d4 at every level.

name: Grünfeld Defense
idea: Black lets White build a pawn center with the plan of undermining it immediately with pieces.
plans: After cxd5 Nxd5, Black targets the c3 and d4 pawns with ...Bg7 and ...c5.
White often gets a large center but must be careful it doesn't become a target.
A hypermodern classic — pawns first, then pressure, rather than direct occupation of the center.

name: English Opening
idea: White plays a Sicilian Defense with an extra tempo, aiming for a flexible, strategically rich middlegame.
plans: White can transpose into many structures — Sicilian-like, King's Indian-like or symmetric setups.
Central pawn breaks (d4 for White, ...d5 for Black) are typically well-timed rather than immediate.
A flexible first move that avoids heavy early theory while staying fully sound.

name: Scandinavian Defense
idea: Black challenges the center immediately, accepting an early queen excursion in exchange for simple, direct play.
plans: White gains development tempo by harassing the black queen with Nc3 and d4.
Black aims to finish development quickly with ...Nf6, ...c6 and ...Bf5 or ...Bg4.
A practical, low-theory way to meet 1.e4 that still gives Black active piece play.

name: Pirc Defense
idea: Black delays central contact, fianchettoing the bishop and preparing to strike at White's center from the flank.
plans: Black typically follows with Bg7, O-O and c5 or e5 breaks.
White often builds a broad center with f4 or Be3/Qd2, aiming for a kingside attack.
Similar in spirit to the King's Indian — flexible, hypermodern and combative.

name: Alekhine's Defense
idea: Black provokes White's pawns forward, planning to attack the overextended center later with pieces and pawn breaks.
plans: White gains space quickly but must guard against the center becoming weak.
Black chips away with ...dxe5, ...c5 or ...Nb6, targeting overextended pawns.
A provocative, hypermodern try that rewards precise piece play over material grabs.

name: London System
idea: White sets up a simple, solid structure (pawns on d4/e3, bishop developed before e3) that works against almost any Black setup.
plans: White follows up with e3, Bd3 (or Be2), Nbd2, c3 and often h3 for a safe, flexible structure.
Because the setup is so consistent, White can focus on plans rather than memorizing sharp theory.
A popular, low-maintenance opening choice at club level and beyond.

name: Vienna Game
idea: White develops the knight before the bishop, keeping options open for an aggressive f4 push or a quiet fianchetto setup.
plans: White can choose between the sharp Vienna Gambit (f4) or the calmer fianchetto with g3 and Bg2.
Black usually meets it with solid development — ...Bc5, ...d6 or ...Nc6.
A flexible way to reach both quiet and sharp middlegames from the same first moves.

name: Scotch Game
idea: White opens the center immediately, trading a pawn for quick piece activity and open lines.
plans: White's knight on d4 is centralized but can become a target, so timing Nc3 or Nb5 matters.
Black develops naturally with ...Bc5 or ...Bb4, fighting for the initiative.
Leads to open, tactical positions rather than the slow maneuvering of the Ruy Lopez.

name: Petrov's Defense
idea: Black mirrors White's attack on e5 instead of defending e5 directly, aiming for quick equality and a symmetrical, safe game.
plans: Both sides typically finish development quickly, often heading for a balanced middlegame.
White sometimes avoids the main line entirely with quieter tries like the Three Knights setup.
A reliable choice for players who want to neutralize 1.e4 with minimal risk.

name: Catalan Opening
idea: White combines a Queen's Gambit pawn structure with a fianchettoed bishop on g2, pressuring the long diagonal and d5/c6.
plans: White often regains a pawn on c4 naturally thanks to pressure from the g2-bishop.
Black looks to complete development safely and challenge the long diagonal with ...c6 or ...dxc4.
A strategically rich opening favored by many elite players for its long-term pressure.
